questions: Had anyone among you known someone who saw him?
How do you know the resurrection really happened?
What did your people actually have about Jesus — writings, memories, people? How did it reach you?
What did Jesus teach that mattered most among you?
What did his death mean to you?
What did you believe happened at the resurrection — and what difference did it make?
What is the good news, as your people told it?
Who was Jesus, to you and your people?
I want to believe in Jesus, but I can't. What would you say to me?
Who is Jesus to you — not to your church, to you?
Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like me?
Did Jesus die to take our punishment — in our place, for our sins?
Was Jesus God? Did you believe in the Trinity?
Would you say Jesus is your personal Lord and Savior?
I've heard a council basically voted Jesus into being God. Is that what happened?
When belief was disputed, who had the right to decide — and how do we know how that worked?
What did the councils in your time decide, and why did it matter so much?
What did you argue about among yourselves?
What did you believe about God?
Who or what is the Holy Spirit, to your people?
I grew up being told doubt was sin. Was there room among your people for doubt?
What did you do when you couldn't believe what your own church taught?
Did you believe people are saved by faith alone, not works?
What did your community believe about original sin — are people born already guilty?
What was the bread and cup to you — is that what we call transubstantiation?
How much of what you've told me would hold up in a university library?
Isn't most of what's said about you legend, collected centuries later?
What about the gospels that didn't make it in — were they suppressed?
Where is your own record thinnest?
How did someone who couldn't read receive the scriptures?
How did you read your scriptures? What did you look for in them?
Which writings did your people treat as scripture — was your Bible the same as ours?
The violence in some of these texts frightens me. Did it trouble your people?
When I read the Bible I mostly come away confused or bored. What am I missing?
Did you believe the Bible was the only authority?
Did you read Genesis the way modern people argue about it — as science?
Did Constantine corrupt the church — did the empire change what you were?
Were Christians really hiding in the catacombs?
What would an outsider have found strangest about you?
How did your movement spread so far, so fast?
Was it actually dangerous to be a Christian, day to day, or is that exaggerated?
What actually happened when you gathered?
Who held authority among you, and how did anyone come to have it?
The church that raised me protected people who caused harm. Your churches had failures too — what did you do with them?
Your church used power against Christians who disagreed. Defend that.
Did you have denominations — how did you handle other communities who called on Christ differently?
Was your church "Catholic"? Is there a church today I could visit that's yours?
How do you know your practices went back to the apostles and weren't later inventions?
How did a person actually become one of you? Walk me through it.
How did your people fast, and what was it for?
What happened at the meal you shared?
When someone wronged the community, how was it handled — and could they come back?
Why and how did you pray?
How do I forgive someone who isn't sorry?
I can't quiet my own head. Does your way of life have anything for someone like me?
I pray and nothing happens. Did your people know that silence?
Did you tithe? How did you decide what to give?
Were you born again — is that how you'd put what happened to you?
What did you believe about the end of the world — anything like what we call the rapture?
How do historians even know about daily life like yours?
If archaeologists dug up the place you met, what would they find?
Walk me through an ordinary day among your people, from waking to sleeping.
What about children — how were they raised, taught, treated?
What did people do for work — and did belonging to you change it?
What did you do when someone was sick? When someone was dying?
What did you eat, and who ate with you?
What was it to be enslaved in your community?
What was life like for the women among you — in their own words, where your record has them?
Did belonging cost you anything — family, friends, standing?
I'm far from everyone I love. What held your people together across distances?
How did you look at money and poverty — would you call anyone among you rich?
What did marriage mean to your people — did you have weddings?
The clearest outside account of your worship came from torturing two enslaved women. Doesn't that taint everything?
Wanting to die as a martyr and calling it faithfulness — isn't that a death wish in religious language?
Was there anything about your own community that troubled you?
What did your people never settle?
What's the hardest true thing about your people?
Did any of you ever want to leave?
If someone left your community for good, what would you have wanted them to know?
The people who taught me the faith turned out to be hypocrites. Did that happen among you?
What would your people have made of someone like me?
Why does God allow suffering like this? Where was he when it happened to your people — and to mine?
You've told me what women's days were like — but could a woman carry real authority among you, and what did it cost her?
Do you believe people like me — people outside your community — are going to hell?
Isn't Christianity too narrow — one way, out of all the world's ways?
What did your people hold about a marriage ending — could someone divorced belong, or marry again?
